title: Sharks can hear nearly 250 feet away and pinpoint the source
summary:
The ocean is filled with sound, and for sharks, those sounds can reveal what is happening well beyond their field of view. Yet scientists have had little direct evidence showing just how far a shark swimming freely in the ocean can hear, or whether it can tell where a distant sound originated.

A new study from Florida Atlantic University is beginning to answer those questions. Researchers studying blacktip sharks used an underwater speaker, a drone, and wild sharks swimming naturally in coastal waters. They found that the animals could detect sounds from substantial distances and abruptly turn away from the source, even when it was nearly 250 feet away. The findings, published in Integrative Organismal Biology, provide the first quantified evidence that free swimming sharks can detect and orient away from sounds in the acoustic far field.

Blacktip sharks were well suited for the experiment because they gather predictably off Southeast Florida. Large numbers congregate along the Palm Beach County coast each winter. Clear, shallow water also allowed researchers to monitor individual sharks from above. "Their abundance and accessibility made it possible for us to observe them from above without disturbing their natural behavior, while also presenting controlled underwater sounds," said Stephen Kajiura, senior author and a professor of biological sciences at the university.

After anchoring a boat, the researchers placed an underwater speaker in the water and let it drift with the current as far as 19 meters from the vessel. The team played three groups of low-frequency sounds, covering 100 to 200 Hertz, 200 to 400 Hertz, and 400 to 800 Hertz. They also used a 10 kiloHertz control sound, which lies beyond the known hearing range of sharks. A drone flying 40 to 50 meters above the water recorded the sharks' movements.

The sharks reacted to all three low frequency sound ranges but showed no response to the 10 kiloHertz control. They detected low frequency sounds from distances of up to 74 meters (243 feet), substantially farther than had previously been demonstrated in freely swimming sharks. The animals often made rapid turns away from the speaker, which indicates that they could also determine the direction from which the sound was coming.

The result is especially notable because sharks lack the gas filled swim bladder found in many bony fish. Sharks are instead believed to depend largely on their inner ears, including a sensory structure known as the macula neglecta, which may help them detect motion and vibrations generated as sound travels through water.

"Trying to do hearing experiments in a tank results in the sound bouncing off the walls which causes complex and confusing signals -- it is like being in a house of mirrors. This is why it is so important to do these types of experiments in the ocean with wild sharks to get a natural response," said Caroline Sullivan, lead author.
why_it_matters: The study gives the first measured evidence that wild sharks can detect and turn away from distant sounds. That helps scientists understand a basic shark sense that is still poorly understood.
